evidence.excerpt:
Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed
assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human–AI collaboration offers a further
mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments,
and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human–AI coordination,
and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems
remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the9A Frameworkfor Human–AI Collaborative
Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. Theorganizationlayer
specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who
holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). Thecoordinationlayer addresses how
participants access relevant research information

evidence.excerpt:
Scientific inquiry develops through contributions that are proposed, tested, questioned, revised,
and sometimes abandoned. Research on the social epistemology of science emphasizes critical inter-
action and responsiveness to criticism as conditions for collective inquiry [ 17]. These contributions
may introduce new hypotheses, evidence, methods, or objections that require further examination.
For collaborative scientific work to progress, participants need to determine how such contributions
are handled and preserve the reasoning behind consequential decisions. We useaccountabilityto
describe this process: scientific contributions and the responses to them remain traceable, including
what was examined, what concerns were raised, and why particular conclusions or actions were
retained, revised, or rejected.
We describe this process through a recurringAccountability Loop(Figure 2).

evidence.excerpt:
The framework is conceptual, and its proposed relationships have yet to be tested in real scientific
settings. Scientific domains differ in research duration, task risks, available evidence, and dependence
on expert judgment, so appropriate activity granularity, authorization thresholds, and coordination
intensity may vary across contexts. Explicit information sharing, review, and record-keeping also
impose computational and human costs. For bounded, low-risk, and easily verifiable tasks, simple
AI assistance or predominantly autonomous execution may be more appropriate than elaborate
collaborative arrangements. More broadly, widespread reliance on similar AI models across research
teams may also raise concerns about convergence in scientific questions, methods, and research
directions. Such collective effects raise broader questions of epistemic responsibility [20].

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: No optimization loop or scored evaluation is present, so there is no signal reuse to assess.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Not applicable; the manuscript reports no quantitative headline outcome and instead validates its framework through qualitative mapping of existing systems and an illustrative open-source workflow.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; this is a conceptual framework paper that synthesizes organizational, coordination, and evaluation principles rather than training, tuning, or optimizing any model or system.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The claims are carefully aligned with the conceptual nature of the contribution, avoiding unwarranted claims of empirical superiority while explicitly addressing trade-offs, governance challenges, and implementation overhead [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0057, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0068].
primary.evaluation_assessment: As a conceptual/theoretical framework paper, the primary validation comes from mapping existing systems (Virtual Lab, AutoResearchClaw, Co-Scientist) and providing open-source illustrative implementation materials rather than conducting benchmarked empirical experiments [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0034, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0035, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0065].

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: No quantitative model optimization loop is evaluated; existing systems are analyzed through qualitative conceptual mapping.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Not applicable; the paper assesses existing literature and illustrative system mappings qualitatively rather than scoring against an optimization metric.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; this is a conceptual and taxonomy paper synthesizing organizational principles rather than training or optimizing a machine learning model.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly disclose that the framework is conceptual and remains to be empirically tested in live scientific pipelines across diverse domain risks and time horizons [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0068].
primary.method_assessment: The manuscript grounds its conceptual synthesis thoroughly in foundational literature across team cognition, human factors, philosophy of science, and multi-agent AI systems [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0006, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0017, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0021]. Each of the nine conceptual pillars is clearly defined and operationalized through representations like the activity-actor-authority mapping and the accountability loop [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0033, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0041].
primary.quality_rationale: The paper makes a coherent, well-structured, and substantive conceptual contribution to understanding and designing human-AI collaborative workflows in scientific discovery. The synthesis of organization, coordination, and evaluation layers fills a recognized conceptual gap in the literature, fully supported by appropriate theoretical positioning and realistic scoping.
primary.scoped_contribution: A conceptual framework (the 9A Framework) organizing Human-AI Collaborative Science across three interconnected layers: organization (Activity, Actor, Authority), coordination (Awareness, Accountability, Adaptability), and evaluation (Achievement, Attribution, Assurance) [Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0002, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0003, Eec0e7eff036b2f31-B0008].
